title: Mumbai's Lalbaugcha Raja Food Waste to Power Civic Hospitals During Ganeshotsav
excerpt: Under BMC's 'Prasad to Power' plan, 8–10 tonnes of wet waste from Mumbai's most famous Ganesh pandal will be converted into electricity for municipal hospitals across the 11-day festival.
body:
• Mumbai's civic body has launched a first-of-its-kind "Prasad to Power" initiative, converting wet waste from the Lalbaugcha Raja Ganesh Mandal into electricity for municipal hospitals during Ganeshotsav 2026.
  • About 8–10 metric tonnes of food and organic waste will be collected and processed each day across the 11-day festival.
  • The waste is expected to generate roughly 7,744 units of electricity, offsetting power demand at civic hospitals.
  • The move signals a wider BMC push to divert festival waste from landfills — Mumbai cleared more than 900 tonnes of post-festival waste in 2024.

Prasad to Power

The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation will turn the food waste from Mumbai's most famous Ganesh pandal into electricity for its hospitals. Under the "Prasad to Power" plan, wet waste generated at the Lalbaugcha Raja Ganesh Mandal — leftover prasad, food offerings and organic waste from the pandal's kitchens and feeding operations — will be collected daily during the 11-day Ganesh festival and processed to produce power for municipal hospitals.

Officials estimate 8–10 metric tonnes of food and organic waste will be generated at the pandal each day, translating to about 7,744 units of electricity over the course of the festival. The civic body describes the effort as a first-of-its-kind initiative linking a religious celebration directly to public infrastructure.

"Around 8–10 metric tonnes of food and organic waste will be processed daily during the 11-day festival, generating about 7,744 units of electricity."

— The BMC's "Prasad to Power" plan

Context & Background

The Lalbaugcha Raja pandal in central Mumbai is among the city's most visited Ganesh mandals, drawing lakhs of devotees each day during the festival. That footfall generates enormous volumes of food waste: the kitchens that prepare prasad and meals for visitors, the offerings devotees leave behind, and the organic refuse from stalls around the pandal.

Festival waste has long been a headache for the BMC. After the 2024 Ganesh festival, the civic body cleared more than 900 tonnes of waste from immersion sites across the city — 363 metric tonnes of solid waste and 550 metric tonnes of floral nirmalya sent for composting, according to a DevDiscourse report on the clean-up. Mumbai generates roughly 6,400 tonnes of municipal solid waste every day, and around 700 tonnes still reaches the Deonar dumping ground daily without scientific treatment, per civic data cited by Praja Foundation.

The BMC already processes most of the city's waste at its Kanjurmarg integrated facility, where bioreactor technology converts organic waste into biogas. The Lalbaugcha Raja initiative extends that waste-to-energy approach to a single, high-visibility source: one of India's most famous festival pandals.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers are modest at city scale — roughly 90 to 110 tonnes of organic waste diverted from landfills over 11 days, and under 8,000 units of electricity — but the symbolism and the template matter. Wet waste processed through biomethanation is broken down by microorganisms into biogas, which fuels generators; capturing it at the source keeps methane-emitting organic matter out of dumping grounds and turns a disposal cost into a usable resource.

Directing the power to municipal hospitals is a deliberate choice. Civic hospitals run around the clock, and even a small offset of their electricity demand during the festival weeks is measurable relief for the BMC's own power bills. The bigger test is operational: segregating and transporting 8–10 tonnes of wet waste daily from one of Mumbai's most crowded locations, in monsoon-season conditions, without disrupting the festival itself.

If the logistics hold, the BMC has a replicable model. Thousands of sarvajanik mandals across Mumbai and Maharashtra generate comparable food waste each Ganeshotsav; a pilot that works at Lalbaugcha Raja could be extended to other large pandals in future years.

Diaspora Angle

Ganeshotsav is among the most closely followed Indian festivals in the diaspora — many NRIs plan Mumbai visits around it, and millions more watch the Lalbaugcha Raja darshan from abroad. An initiative that pairs devotion with sustainability gives the diaspora a concrete example of Indian cities solving environmental problems through cultural institutions rather than around them, and it offers a talking point for parents explaining both faith and civic responsibility to the next generation.

What's Next

The 11-day festival runs from Ganesh Chaturthi on September 14 through Anant Chaturdashi, when the Lalbaugcha Raja idol will be immersed at Girgaon Chowpatty. The BMC will collect waste from the pandal daily through the festival; after immersion, the civic body is expected to publish the actual electricity yield, which will determine whether "Prasad to Power" expands beyond a pilot. Watch for announcements on whether other major mandals are brought into the program for next year's festival.
